steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: The residents of Sierra should vote in favor of a local tax to fund construction of the proposed road.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
The builders won't finish the Glen Veil complex unless a road connecting it to Sierra is built. So the road is required for the complex.

If the complex is completed, it will strengthen Sierra's economy, and a stronger economy would benefit every Sierra resident.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Line up what the premises give us against what the conclusion asks for.

The premises are all about benefit. The complex is waiting on the road, the finished complex strengthens the economy, and the stronger economy helps every resident.

The conclusion is about duty: residents should vote for a tax. Nothing in the premises says that benefiting from something means you ought to vote to fund it. That's the new idea the conclusion brings in, and it's the gap.

There's also a cost the developer never weighs. A tax costs every resident something too. The developer simply treats the benefit as enough to settle the vote. A principle that justifies this reasoning has to make that move for us.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body:
On a justify-the-reasoning principle, the answer usually has the shape If Evidence, then Conclusion, written in general terms. Here the evidence boils down to benefit, and the conclusion is a vote for a tax. So predict:

would benefit from a construction project → should vote for a tax that funds it

The right side has to say residents should vote in favor. A principle that only tells us when not to vote for a tax, or who should pay one, can't deliver that conclusion.

notes.body: A fires only when a project is "necessary in order to strengthen a town’s economy." The road is necessary for the complex, but nothing says the complex is the only way to strengthen Sierra's economy, so we can't show the road is necessary for a stronger economy. The trigger isn't established, and A never touches the benefit to every resident that the developer argues from.

This is the tempting one, because it talks about results that "benefit all of those residents," which is exactly what the developer established. But read the direction. B says residents "should not vote in favor" of the tax unless everyone benefits. That makes benefit to all a requirement for a yes vote:

a yes vote is acceptable → the project benefits all residents

The developer has the right side, not the left. Meeting a requirement only keeps a yes vote from being ruled out. It never tells residents they should vote yes, and that is the conclusion we need.

C only applies once a town is funding a project, and then it compares a tax with debt. The developer's question is whether residents should back this tax at all. C never mentions benefit, so the developer's evidence can't trigger it, and its outcome is about the form of funding, not about how residents should vote.

D is about who "should be required to pay" a tax. The developer's conclusion is about how residents should vote, not who gets billed. And D only limits payment to beneficiaries. Knowing everyone benefits makes everyone eligible to pay, but being eligible to pay is not a reason anyone should vote for the tax.

E is the If Evidence, then Conclusion principle we predicted. Its left side, anyone "who would benefit from the results of a construction project," matches the developer's evidence: the finished complex depends on the road, and the complex strengthens the economy and benefits every Sierra resident. Its right side, "should vote in favor of a local tax to fund that project," is the conclusion almost word for word.

The move to repeat: when the conclusion says someone should do something and the premises only describe facts, look for the principle whose left side is built from the premises and whose right side is the should. E supplies the missing bridge from benefit to duty.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes; B and D notes argued speculative counter-uses instead of the conditional direction, and the Goal was a bulleted list with no prediction.

steps.label: Main Conclusion
steps.body: We should not be persuaded by Graham's argument.

steps.label: Premise
steps.body: People sleep, and at least sometimes when sleeping they are truly happy, even though they are not doing anything.

steps.label: Opposing Point (Graham's conclusion)
steps.body: The best life is a life that is full of activity.

steps.label: Opposing Point (Graham's premise)
steps.body: A person is truly happy only when doing something.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Two arguments are stacked here. Graham's: a person is truly happy only when doing something, so the best life is full of activity. The philosopher's: we shouldn't be persuaded by Graham's argument, because people are sometimes truly happy while sleeping, when they aren't doing anything.

Which part of Graham's argument does the sleep claim hit? Graham's premise is a conditional:

truly happy → doing something

A sleeper who is truly happy while doing nothing has the left side without the right side. That's a counterexample to the premise.

Notice what the philosopher does not claim. The philosopher never says the best life isn't full of activity. The conclusion is only that Graham's argument shouldn't persuade us. Knocking out a premise is enough for that, because an argument with a false premise doesn't establish its conclusion, even if the conclusion happens to be true.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The claim in the stem is the philosopher's premise, and its job is to show that Graham's premise is false. Look for an answer that names both pieces: an example, aimed at Graham's premise rather than Graham's conclusion.

notes.body: A gets the owner wrong. Graham's premise is that a person is truly happy only when doing something. The sleep claim contradicts that, so it can't be part of Graham's argument. It belongs to the philosopher, who uses it against Graham.

B names both the form and the target. It is an example: a sleeper who is truly happy while doing nothing is one specific case. And it aims to show that "a premise of Graham’s argument is false": the case breaks Graham's premise that true happiness requires doing something.

The move to repeat on Role questions: when a speaker attacks someone else's argument, ask which part the attack lands on, the premise or the conclusion. Then match the answer to that exact target.

Graham never mentions sleep. The sleeping case is the philosopher's own, and the philosopher relies on it rather than rejecting it. It isn't an analogy either: it is a direct case of happiness without activity, not a comparison to some other situation.

D is the closest trap, because the claim is an example and it is aimed at Graham. But it hits the premise, not the conclusion. A happy sleeper doesn't show that the best life isn't full of activity; a busy life could still be best for other reasons. That's why the philosopher concludes only that we shouldn't be persuaded, not that Graham's conclusion is false.

The main conclusion is that we should not be persuaded by Graham's argument. Ask why we should believe that. Because people are sometimes truly happy while sleeping. The sleep claim answers the why, so it is support for the conclusion, not the conclusion itself.

why: No Evaluate or Goal step, the correct-answer note was a one-line verdict, and wrong-answer notes were bare role labels with no test.

steps.label: Conclusion (it follows that)
steps.body: The sole reason that sexual reproduction has become the rule among both animals and plants is that natural selection has favored some entire species over others.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The evolutionary advantage of sexual reproduction is that it increases the range of genetic variation in a species, which is an advantage for the species as a whole. But an increased range of genetic variation in a species is not advantageous for any individual member of the species.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
"It follows that" marks the last sentence as the conclusion: the sole reason sexual reproduction became the rule is that natural selection favored some entire species over others.

Why should we believe it? The biologist gives two facts that work together. First, the advantage of sexual reproduction is wider genetic variation, which helps the species as a whole. Second, that variation helps no individual member. If the advantage shows up only at the species level, selection among individuals can't explain why sexual reproduction spread. That leaves selection among whole species, which is the conclusion.

Slow down on the "However." It contrasts species with individuals, but it doesn't turn against the biologist. Both sentences are on the conclusion's side. The second one actually does the heavier lifting, since it is what rules out an individual-level explanation.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The stem asks about the second premise, the claim that the variation helps no individual. Predict: a premise that supports the conclusion. Expect an answer as plain as a claim offered in support of the conclusion.

notes.body:
That's the prediction. The claim about individuals is offered as a reason, and the conclusion depends on it: once individuals gain nothing from the variation, the remaining explanation is selection among whole species.

The move to repeat: find the conclusion by its indicator, then ask of the target claim whether it answers why we should believe the conclusion. If it does, it is support, no matter what contrast word introduces it.

B reads the "However" as a turn against the conclusion. The turn is between two premises: good for the species, but not for individuals. Test it: if individuals did benefit, the conclusion would get weaker, because individual selection could then explain the spread. So the claim helps the conclusion. It doesn't cast doubt on it.

The argument never questions this claim. It asserts it and builds on it. A claim the argument is designed to call into question would be something the biologist argues against, and the biologist argues from this one.

The phenomenon the biologist explains is that sexual reproduction "has become the rule among both animals and plants." The target claim isn't that phenomenon. It is a fact about who benefits from genetic variation, used to help explain the spread.

The explanation the argument offers is in the conclusion: natural selection favoring some entire species over others. The target claim helps rule out the rival, individual-level explanation, which is why the species-level one wins. Helping to establish an explanation is not the same as being the explanation.

why: Explicit-Standard register with heavy em dashes; Evaluate only named indicator words, the Goal restated the task, and the B trap was not tied to the However pivot.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Emotion is not nonrational.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
steps.body: Emotion only seems nonrational because language lacks the ability to convey adequate conceptions of emotion.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body:
The words we use to refer to emotions name only very general kinds of inner experience, such as excitement, calm and joy.

Illustration of that: there is no language for describing just how one joy differs from another.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Role and Main Conclusion arguments often put the conclusion right after a pivot that pushes back on someone's view. Here the philosopher opens with how philosophers usually treat emotions, as nonrational, then pivots with "But": emotion is not nonrational. That's the main conclusion.

Everything after it is support, in layers. Why believe emotion isn't nonrational? Because it only seems that way, since language can't convey adequate conceptions of emotion. Why believe language falls short? Because emotion words name only very general kinds of experience.

Then the last sentence opens with "Thus, for example." Two signals that seem to fight. "Thus" usually marks something that follows; "for example" marks an illustration. Both fit. If emotion words are only general, they can't separate one joy from another, so the last sentence follows from the general claim. And it is offered as one concrete case of that general claim. It isn't where the argument is headed. It is a picture of the evidence.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The target claim is a specific case of the general claim about emotion words, and that general claim supports the main conclusion through the middle step about language. Predict an answer that calls it an example or illustration of a supporting claim, with only an indirect link to the main conclusion.

notes.body: The phenomenon the argument explains is that emotion seems nonrational. An example of that would be a case of someone treating an emotion as nonrational. The joy claim is nothing like that. It is a case of language being too general, which is part of the explanation, not part of what gets explained.

The main conclusion is "emotion is not nonrational," right after the "But." The joy claim is offered to help support it, so it can't be it. "Thus" is the bait. Here it shows the joy claim follows from the general point about emotion words, and "for example" shows it illustrates that point. A main conclusion is where the argument ends up, and this sentence is a step on the way.

C traces the support chain exactly. One joy versus another is "a specific instance," a single case. It is "illustrating a general claim," the claim that emotion words name only very general kinds of experience. And it is "thereby indirectly supporting the conclusion," because that general claim backs the point about language, which backs the conclusion that emotion isn't nonrational.

The move to repeat: when a role answer says indirectly, check that a middle claim sits between the target and the conclusion. Here one does, so indirectly is accurate.

A concession grants something to the other side. The other side says emotion is nonrational. The joy claim grants nothing to that view. It supports the philosopher's account of why emotion only seems nonrational, so it works against the opposing view.

E is tempting because the joy claim sits close to the explanation. But the explanation offered for why emotion seems nonrational is that "language lacks the ability to convey adequate conceptions of emotion." The joy claim is one case under the general point about emotion words, which in turn backs that explanation. It illustrates the support. It isn't the explanation itself.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes; Evaluate misquoted the stimulus and used slang, the A note used a gendered pronoun for the philosopher, and the intermediate conclusion had a typo.

steps.label: Intermediate Conclusion
steps.body: For early humans who moved from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to agriculture, the transition must have been traumatic.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: There would have been increased incidence of disease and injury and a more homogeneous diet lacking vital nutrients more easily obtainable from the richly varied diet of hunter-gatherers.

steps.label: Main Conclusion
steps.body: Groups that made the transition were likely motivated by certain benefits that accompany the settled life of the agriculturist, such as opportunities for the accumulation of wealth by those with specialized social roles.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
Start with the indicator. "Thus" opens the last sentence, so that's a conclusion: groups that switched to agriculture were likely motivated by benefits of settled life.

Now test the first sentence the way we test any candidate: why should we believe the transition was traumatic? The second sentence answers. More disease and injury, and a diet lacking vital nutrients. So the first sentence has support of its own.

Does it support anything? Yes. Why think the groups were drawn by benefits like wealth? Because the switch was traumatic, and the argument's thought is that groups wouldn't accept that kind of hardship without something to gain. So the traumatic claim is supported by the second sentence and supports the last one. That makes it an intermediate conclusion.

The first sentence looks like a classic first-sentence conclusion. It is a conclusion, just not the main one. "Thus" settles which one is main.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The quoted claim is an intermediate conclusion, but the answer may not use that phrase. It might call the claim a premise that has support of its own. Look for an answer that says the claim is supported and also supports the main conclusion.

notes.body:
Here is the intermediate conclusion in disguise. The claim is "a premise" because it supports the main conclusion, and "another premise is offered as support" because the disease, injury and diet sentence backs it up.

The move to repeat: on Role questions, run two checks on the target claim. Does something support it? Does it support something? Two yeses means an intermediate conclusion, whatever words the answer uses for it.

B says the claim "plays no logical role." Remove it and see what happens. The second sentence would be left with nothing to prove, and the conclusion would lose the hardship that makes the benefits worth mentioning. A claim that holds the argument together is not background.

C is the trap for anyone who stopped after the first sentence. It gets half right: the claim does act as a premise for the conclusion. The failure is the second half. Ask why we should believe the transition was traumatic. The very next sentence answers: more disease and injury, and a diet lacking vital nutrients. That is support, so "no support is offered" is false.

The conclusion of the argument as a whole comes after "Thus": groups that switched were likely motivated by the benefits of settled life. The traumatic claim is a step toward that point. It is a conclusion, but only an intermediate one.

Nothing in the argument pushes back on the traumatic claim. The anthropologist supports it with evidence and then builds on it. A claim the argument seeks to rebut would be followed by reasons it is wrong, and here every reason points the other way.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes; no Goal step, Evaluate only asserted the role, and the correct note hedged instead of teaching the two-check test.

steps.label: Conclusion (Therefore)
steps.body: A successful legal system prohibits only those few behaviors that citizens find absolutely intolerable.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The purpose of laws in a legal system is to deter bad actions by threatening punishment if you perform them, but this only works if people think they're likely to get punished for committing those actions, and the more behaviors that are criminalized, the less likely someone will be caught and punished.

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Role and Main Conclusion, it pays to check the first sentence and any pivot before trusting the end. Here neither holds up. The first sentence, about the purpose of a law, gets no support from anything else. The "But" sentence, about the odds of being caught dropping as prohibitions multiply, isn't supported either. A claim with no support can't be a conclusion.

That leaves the "Therefore" sentence, and this time it really is the main conclusion: a successful legal system prohibits only the few behaviors citizens find absolutely intolerable. Why believe that? Laws work by threatening punishment. The threat works only if people think they're likely to be punished. And the more kinds of acts are prohibited, the less likely punishment becomes. Keep the list short, and the threat stays believable.

The first sentence is the starting point of that chain. Nothing supports it, and it supports the conclusion.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The target is the first sentence. It supports the conclusion and has no support of its own. Predict: a premise.

notes.body: A invents a conclusion. The scholar never mentions police officers or how many a legal system needs. The stated conclusion is about limiting the number of prohibited behaviors, and the first sentence supports that. An answer built on a conclusion the argument never draws can't describe a role in it.

The conclusion comes after "Therefore": a successful legal system prohibits only a few intolerable behaviors. Ask whether anything supports the first sentence. Nothing does. It is a starting point, and a claim with nothing behind it can't be the conclusion.

C matches the prediction. The first sentence starts the chain: laws deter through threatened punishment, the threat needs believable punishment, more prohibitions make punishment less likely, so prohibit only the intolerable. Nothing earlier props it up.

The move to repeat: two questions settle most Role answers. Is the claim supported? Does it support something? Here the answers are no and yes. That combination is a plain premise.

D is the trap for students who expect Role questions to ask about an intermediate conclusion. An intermediate conclusion has both jobs: it gets support and gives support. The first sentence gives support but gets none. The next two sentences don't argue for it; they build on it. With no support coming in, it is a premise.

The scholar doesn't attack this view. The scholar builds on it. If the argument were designed to discredit the idea that laws deter by threatening punishment, we'd see reasons against it. Instead, the rest of the argument depends on it being true.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes and repetitive 90-word notes; Evaluate overstated that conclusion indicators always mark a conclusion, and the Conclusion step had a typo.

steps.label: Conclusion (Hence)
steps.body: There's unlikely to be a widespread, grassroots effort for new, more restrictive air pollution controls at this time.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: People generally notice and are concerned about only the most obvious public health problems. And most people are currently well aware that contaminated water is a much more widespread threat to the community than is air pollution (such as ozone).

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Main Conclusion and Role, the conclusion is usually found earlier than the support, but in this case it was the final sentence, signified by "Hence". Because this is Role, we want to be highly alert for whether that "Hence" is actually just an Intermediate Conclusion, but in this case we can tell it's the main conclusion because the 1st and 3rd claim combine to support this 4th claim. There are four claims in this argument, and structurally they go in this order:
    1. Premise
    2. Counterpoint (although)
    3. Premise
    4. Conclusion (hence)
    We're being asked about the first sentence, which was one of the two premises for the conclusion in the final sentence.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The stem asks about the first sentence, one of the two premises. Predict: a premise that supports the conclusion that a widespread grassroots push for stricter air pollution controls is unlikely right now.

notes.body: A aims the first sentence at the wrong claim. The water claim isn't argued for. It is reported as something most people already know. The first sentence teams up with it instead: people care only about the most obvious problems, and right now the obvious one is water, so no grassroots push on air pollution. It supports the conclusion, not the water claim.

B names the target and the destination. The first sentence is a general rule about attention, and the argument applies it: people care only about the most obvious health problems, water is the problem people are aware of, so air pollution won't draw a grassroots effort now. The first sentence is a premise for the "Hence" claim.

The move to repeat: when an argument pairs a general rule with a specific fact, the rule is usually a premise the conclusion applies. Check where the rule is aimed, and match the answer to that claim.

C says the first sentence explains why people are aware of the water problem. The argument never asks why. It states the awareness as a fact and uses it. The first sentence is about what people pay attention to, and the argument aims it at the conclusion about air pollution controls.

The "indisputable evidence" belongs to the ozone claim in the second sentence, about danger to severe asthmatics. The first sentence is about what people notice, not about whether ozone is dangerous. It offers no evidence about ozone at all.

The main conclusion follows "Hence": a widespread grassroots effort for stricter air pollution controls is unlikely now. Ask why we should believe that. Partly because people notice only the most obvious problems. The first sentence answers the why, so it is support, not the conclusion.

why: Breakdown was sound, but every note was a 100-plus-word Explicit-Standard paragraph with em dashes and repetition, and the Goal put a paraphrase in quotation marks.

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.body: Our mastery of Latin and Ancient Greek is at best imperfect.

steps.label: Evidence
steps.body: The best students of a modern language can immerse themselves in a country where that language is spoken in order to attain nearly perfect knowledge. But you can't travel back in time (to ancient Greece) to spend a year at Plato's Academy (immersing yourself in the ancient Greek language).

steps.label: Evaluate
steps.body:
On Role and Main Conclusion, the conclusion very often sits in the first sentence or right after a pivot. So hear the first sentence as a possible opinion: our mastery of Latin and Ancient Greek is "at best imperfect." If the rest of the passage supports it, it's the main conclusion.

It does. The second sentence sets up a contrast. On one side, the best students of a modern language can immerse themselves where it is spoken and get close to perfect knowledge. On the other side, you can't spend a year abroad at Plato's Academy. Immersion is open for living languages and closed for ancient ones. That contrast is why the classicist thinks mastery of the ancient languages falls short.

Notice what the Plato's Academy line is. It isn't a general statement that ancient immersion is impossible. It is one vivid case that makes the point.

steps.label: Goal
steps.body: The target claim is the second half of the contrast, given as a concrete case. Predict: support for the first sentence, possibly described as an example or as one side of a comparison.

notes.body: The main conclusion is the first sentence: our mastery of the ancient languages is imperfect. Ask why we should believe it, and the Plato's Academy line is part of the answer. A claim that answers the why for another claim is support, not the main conclusion.

B describes the claim's job piece by piece. There is "a contrast": modern-language students can immerse themselves, and students of ancient languages can't. The claim points it up "by example": the Plato's Academy line makes the second side concrete with one trip nobody can take. And it is a contrast "from which the conclusion is drawn": imperfect mastery follows from it.

The move to repeat: abstract role answers are easiest to check in pieces. Match each phrase to a specific part of the passage, and reject the answer if any piece has nothing to land on.

C says the claim has "no logical relation" to the conclusion. Remove it and see. The second sentence would describe only what modern-language students can do, with nothing to compare against. The contrast that supports the conclusion would disappear, so the claim is doing logical work.

D starts well, because the claim is support. The problem is "guarantees the truth." Even granting that you can't visit Plato's Academy, the conclusion needs more: that immersion, or something like it, is needed for nearly perfect knowledge. The modern-language sentence only says the best students may get there through immersion. The claim helps the conclusion. It doesn't force it.

An ancillary conclusion would be a claim the argument supports on its way to the main point. Nothing in the passage argues that you can't travel back in time. It is offered as plain fact. A claim with nothing supporting it can't be a conclusion of any kind.

why: Explicit-Standard register with em dashes and 100-word repetitive notes; Evaluate used a gendered pronoun for the classicist and the Goal predicted a plain premise without anticipating the example-and-contrast wording.
